Where it began

Michael Clarke was born in Liverpool, in the western suburbs of Sydney, on 2 April 1981. His father ran an indoor cricket centre in the town, and that is where the boy sharpened his batting after school. He did everything else left-handed, writing and bowling included, yet trained himself to bat right-handed.

He was 17 when he first played for New South Wales, in December 1999, when the touring Indians came to the SCG. A season in English league cricket followed in 2002, at Ramsbottom, where he made the first double hundred the Lancashire League had ever seen.

The player

Few Test careers have started better. On debut at Bangalore in 2004 he danced down the pitch to India's spinners and made 151; a few weeks later, in his first home Test, at the Gabba, he made 141. No Australian before him had made hundreds on debut both away and at home. He was player of the match both times.

He played 115 Tests from 2004 to 2015 and made 8,643 runs at 49.11, with 28 hundreds and 27 fifties, and held 134 catches, many of them at slip. His great year was 2012. At Sydney, in the hundredth Test on the ground, he made 329 not out, beating a ground record that had stood for more than a century, and a few weeks later he made 210 at Adelaide. Before him only Don Bradman and Wally Hammond had made a triple and a double hundred in the same series. By the end of that year he had become the first batter to make four Test double hundreds in a calendar year.

What made him special

Clarke was beautiful to watch against spin, light on his feet and happy to meet the ball before it could turn. As a captain, from 2011 to 2015, he was bold, always looking for a way to win from the first ball. He led Australia in 47 Tests and won 24 of them, including a 5–0 sweep of the 2013–14 Ashes. In 2015 he captained Australia to the World Cup and top-scored in the final with 74.

His start was so bright that the next part was a test of its own. He lost his place late in 2005, went away, rebuilt his defence to play with a straighter bat, and came back to make hundreds in successive Ashes Tests a year later. He was never really out of the side again.

Away from the middle

He won the Allan Border Medal four times, was chosen as one of Wisden's Cricketers of the Year in 2010 and as Wisden's leading cricketer in the world for 2012. In 2020 he became an Officer of the Order of Australia, and Cricket NSW made him a life member. After playing he wrote an autobiography, My Story, commentated on television for Nine and co-hosted a breakfast sports show on radio.

And finally

He was only ever an occasional left-arm spinner, but in Mumbai in 2004 he took 6 for 9 in a little over six overs. Plenty of full-time bowlers would have been delighted with those figures. Clarke had to settle for them being the best of his career.
